notes.shape: The yield curve is a graph plotting Treasury yields across maturities from 1 month to 30 years, with a normal upward slope reflecting higher yields for longer maturities due to risk and time preferences. An inverted yield curve, where short-term yields exceed long-term yields, has historically preceded each modern U.S. recession by 6 to 18 months. Currently, the 10-year Treasury yield stands at 4.69% for June 2026, and the 10Y-2Y spread is 0.34 points, indicating a positively sloped curve. This marks a shift from the deepest inversion of 0.0 points during 2022-2024 when the curve was inverted but has since re-steepened above zero.
notes.signal: The 2s10s spread is a key recession indicator, with inversion (negative spread) signaling economic contraction risk. The series spent 2022-2024 inverted before the spread moved back above zero, reflecting an un-inversion. The New York Fed recession probability remains elevated at 31%, emphasizing recession risk despite the un-inverted yield curve. It is notable that the yield curve often un-inverts shortly before a recession, complicating timing signals.
notes.now: Currently, the yield curve’s positive slope at 0.34 points combined with a 31% recession probability suggests heightened caution without definitive recession timing. The re-steepening after a prolonged inversion signals some market relief but does not eliminate recession risk.
